claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: High-speed object recognition presumably relies on feedforward processing, leveraging the hierarchy of features represented in the visual cortex.
claims.source: High-speed object recognition presumably relies on feedforward processing, leveraging the hierarchy of features represented in the visual cortex.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on computational models and neurophysiological understanding.

claims.claim: Neurons in lower areas coding for elementary features rapidly propagate activity to shape selective neurons in higher visual areas.
claims.source: Neurons in lower areas coding for elementary features rapidly propagate activity to shape selective neurons in higher visual areas (Hung et al., 2005; DiCarlo et al., 2012), grouping features into more complex constellations (Roelfsema, 2006)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to neurophysiological studies.

claims.claim: Perceptual grouping can coincide with object recognition.
claims.source: grouping features into more complex constellations (Roelfsema, 2006) so that perceptual grouping coincides with object recognition (Biederman et al., 1987; Nakayama et al., 1989; Driver and Baylis, 1996; Pelli et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: There exist conditions where perceptual grouping requires a slow and serial process.
claims.source: However, there also exist conditions where perceptual grouping requires a slow and serial process (Roelfsema, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Curve tracing is an example of a task that invokes a serial, incremental grouping operation.
claims.source: Curve tracing is an example of a task that invokes such a serial, incremental grouping operation (Jolicoeur et al., 1986; Jolicoeur and Ingleton, 1991; Pringle and Egeth, 1988; Roelfsema and Houtkamp, 2011) when participants group contour elements of an elongated curve.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on curve tracing.

claims.claim: In curve tracing tasks, reaction times increase linearly with the length of the curve.
claims.source: In this task, reaction times increase linearly with the length of the curve.
claims.evidence: This is a well-established finding from curve tracing studies, as shown in Figure 1a.

claims.claim: In curve tracing, attention gradually spreads over the curve until it reaches the target.
claims.source: Subjects first direct their attention to the red fixation point and attention then gradually spreads over the curve until it reaches the green circle (Scholte et al., 2001; Houtkamp et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Curve-tracing is implemented in the visual cortex as the propagation of enhanced neuronal activity over the curve's representation.
claims.source: This process is implemented in the visual cortex as the propagation of enhanced neuronal activity over the curve's representation (Pooresmaeili and Roelfsema, 2014) (Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to neurophysiological work and illustrated in Figure 1b.

claims.claim: Curve-tracing is size invariant.
claims.source: Curve-tracing is size invariant (Jolicoeur and Ingleton, 1991) so that the reaction time of observers depends little on the viewing distance.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Size invariance in curve tracing can be explained if perceptual grouping occurs at multiple levels of the visual cortical hierarchy.
claims.source: Size invariance can be explained if perceptual grouping occurs at multiple levels of the visual cortical hierarchy (Roelfsema and Houtkamp, 2011; Pooresmaeili and Roelfsema, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical explanation supported by citations.

claims.claim: When curves are nearby, perceptual grouping requires the high spatial resolution provided by low-level areas where neurons have small receptive fields.
claims.source: When curves are nearby, perceptual grouping requires the high spatial resolution provided by low-level areas where neurons have small receptive fields (RFs) and horizontal connections interconnect neurons with RFs that are nearby in visual space so that progress is slow.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of visual cortex organization.

claims.claim: If curves are farther apart, neurons in higher areas with larger receptive fields can speed up the grouping process.
claims.source: If curves are farther apart, however, neurons in higher areas can take over and their larger RFs could speed up the grouping process (Pooresmaeili and Roelfsema, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation and is an inference about neural mechanisms.

claims.claim: Size invariance occurs when subjects solve a maze, because paths are followed at a higher speed if the distance between the walls is larger.
claims.source: Size invariance also occurs when subjects solve a maze, because paths are followed at a higher speed if the distance between the walls is larger (Crowe et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: The uniform connectedness hypothesis predicts that image regions with homogenous surface properties are grouped instantaneously.
claims.source: The uniform connectedness hypothesis by Palmer and Rock, 1994 will serve as baseline. These authors suggested that image regions with homogenous surface properties are grouped instantaneously (Palmer and Rock, 1994) so that the reaction time should not depend on the placement of cues within a white region enclosed by a black contour (as in Figure 2a).
claims.evidence: This describes a theoretical prediction from prior literature.

claims.claim: The pixel-by-pixel model predicts that grouping is realized by spreading attention across pixels of the same color at a fixed speed.
claims.source: The second model has been called 'pixel-by-pixel' in the context of curve-tracing (McCormick and Jolicoeur, 1994; Jolicoeur and Ingleton, 1991). Grouping is realized by spreading attention across pixels of the same color, at a fixed speed (Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: This describes a theoretical model with citations to prior work.

claims.claim: In the pixel-by-pixel model, processing time is proportional to the length of the shortest path through the object.
claims.source: Spreading starts at one of the cues and processing time is proportional to the length of the shortest path through the object.
claims.evidence: This describes a prediction of the pixel-by-pixel model.

claims.claim: The growth-cone model predicts that grouping speed depends on the size of homogeneous image regions.
claims.source: The third model is the growth-cone model (Figure 2c), inspired by models for curve tracing (Pooresmaeili and Roelfsema, 2014; McCormick and Jolicoeur, 1994; Jolicoeur et al., 1986) and visual routines (Ullman, 1984; Roelfsema et al., 2000). The growth-cone model predicts that grouping speed depends on the size of homogeneous image regions.
claims.evidence: This describes the growth-cone model with citations to related prior work.

claims.claim: In the growth-cone model, spreading is fast within large regions and slows down in narrow regions.
claims.source: Spreading is fast within large regions and slows down in narrow regions.
claims.evidence: This describes a key prediction of the growth-cone model.

claims.claim: The growth-cone model is scale invariant because the total spreading time does not depend on variations in the overall size of the picture.
claims.source: This model is scale invariant because the total spreading time does not depend on variations in the overall size of the picture, caused e.g. by changes in viewing distance.
claims.evidence: This describes a property of the growth-cone model.

claims.claim: The filling-in model predicts that the grouping signal spreads inwards from the boundaries of the cued object.
claims.source: The fourth model is one where the grouping signal spreads inwards from the boundaries of the cued object so that the response time increases with the distance between the cue and the boundary (Figure 2d) (Komatsu, 2006).
claims.evidence: This describes the filling-in model with a citation.

claims.claim: A filling-in process has been proposed for brightness perception.
claims.source: Such a 'filling-in' process has been proposed for brightness perception (Paradiso and Nakayama, 1991) and texture segregation (Lamme et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: The Euclidean model holds that reaction time depends on the distance between cues, irrespective of the shape of the objects.
claims.source: The fifth and final model is a Euclidean model, which will serve as reference because it is simple. It holds that the reaction time depends on the distance between cues, irrespective of the shape of the objects (Figure 2e).
claims.evidence: This describes the Euclidean model as a reference model.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1A, the average accuracy was 94%.
claims.source: The average accuracy was 94%, without signs of a speed-accuracy trade-off (correlation between RT and accuracy; r=0.17, t(22)=0.80, p>0.4).
claims.evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1A, there were no signs of a speed-accuracy trade-off.
claims.source: The average accuracy was 94%, without signs of a speed-accuracy trade-off (correlation between RT and accuracy; r=0.17, t(22)=0.80, p>0.4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1A, if the two cues fell on the 'same' wedge, RTs were shortest in the center of the wedge and longer near the edges.
claims.source: If the two cues fell on the 'same' wedge, RTs were shortest in the center of the wedge and longer near the edges (repeated-measures ANOVA, Greenhuise-Geisser corrected, F(4.5, 85.7)=10.9, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1A, RTs in the 'different' condition were longer than in the 'same' condition.
claims.source: RTs in the 'different' condition were longer than in the 'same' condition (F(1,19)=19.5, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1A, the growth-cone model accounted for 86% of the variance of the RTs.
claims.source: A regression analysis revealed that the growth-cone model accounted for 86% of the variance of the RTs, which was significantly better than models predicting that RT is constant (p<0.001 bootstrap statistic, see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of the experimental data.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1A, the growth-cone model was significantly better than models predicting that RT is constant.
claims.source: A regression analysis revealed that the growth-cone model accounted for 86% of the variance of the RTs, which was significantly better than models predicting that RT is constant (p<0.001 bootstrap statistic, see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is supported by bootstrap statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The Filling-in model predicted that RT is shortest near the edges, opposite to the RT data in Experiment 1A.
claims.source: The Filling-in model predicted that RT is shortest near the edges, opposite to the RT data.
claims.evidence: This compares model predictions to experimental data.

claims.claim: In the control experiment for Experiment 1, edges did not act as a mask.
claims.source: We did not observe a significant correlation between RT and the distance between cue and edge (r=−0.2, t(30)=−1.31, p>0.1). Thus, the edges did not act as a mask.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of control experiment data.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1B, the average accuracy was 93%.
claims.source: The average accuracy was 93% and we did not obtain evidence for a speed-accuracy trade off (correlation between RT and accuracy, r=0.02; t(62)=0.14, p>0.8).
claims.evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1B, there was no evidence for a speed-accuracy trade-off.
claims.source: The average accuracy was 93% and we did not obtain evidence for a speed-accuracy trade off (correlation between RT and accuracy, r=0.02; t(62)=0.14, p>0.8).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1B, the average RT was higher when the cue was farther from the fixation point.
claims.source: The average RT was higher when the cue was farther from the fixation point and a further delay was observed near the edges (warm colors in Figure 4b), in line with the predictions of the growth-cone model (compare Figure 4b to the lower left panel of Figure 3c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1B, a further delay was observed near the edges.
claims.source: The average RT was higher when the cue was farther from the fixation point and a further delay was observed near the edges (warm colors in Figure 4b), in line with the predictions of the growth-cone model (compare Figure 4b to the lower left panel of Figure 3c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1B, the filling-in model erroneously predicted that RTs are shortest near the edges.
claims.source: The filling-in model erroneously predicted that RTs are shortest near the edges.
claims.evidence: This compares model predictions to experimental data.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1B, the Euclidean model accounted for 49% of the variance.
claims.source: The Euclidean model (and the pixel-by-pixel model, which made the same prediction in this experiment) accounted for 49% of the variance but failed to explain the influence of edge vicinity.
claims.evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1B, the Euclidean model failed to explain the influence of edge vicinity.
claims.source: The Euclidean model (and the pixel-by-pixel model, which made the same prediction in this experiment) accounted for 49% of the variance but failed to explain the influence of edge vicinity.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of model performance based on experimental data.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1B, the growth-cone model accounted for 72% of the variance.
claims.source: The growth-cone model did capture this effect and it accounted for 72% of the variance.
claims.evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1B, the predictions of the growth-cone model were significantly better than those of the other models.
claims.source: The predictions of the growth-cone model were significantly better than those of the other models (all ps<0.01 bootstrap statistic)
claims.evidence: This is supported by bootstrap statistical analysis.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1B, the average speed of perceptual grouping was 22 ms/growth cone (95% confidence interval 17–27 ms).
claims.source: the regression revealed that the average speed of perceptual grouping was 22 ms/growth cone (95% confidence interval 17–27 ms, bootstrap analysis).
claims.evidence: This is derived from regression analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: Grouping of surfaces invokes a serial perceptual grouping process that proceeds fast in homogeneous image regions and slows down near edges.
claims.source: Thus, grouping of surfaces invokes a serial perceptual grouping process that proceeds fast in homogeneous image regions and slows down near edges, in accordance with the growth-cone model.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results of Experiment 1.

claims.claim: Object recognition can provide larger chunks to be grouped at once.
claims.source: Third, does object recognition affect perceptual grouping, because it can provide larger chunks to be grouped at once, as suggested by previous work (Mahoney and Ullman, 1988; Peterson and Gibson, 1994; Vecera and Farah, 1997; Korjoukov et al., 2012)?
claims.evidence: This is a question based on prior research cited.

claims.claim: In Experiment 2 with scrambled cartoons, the RT was shortest for the nearest cue (627 ms) and it increased by 24/30 ms for the more distant cues.
claims.source: The RT was shortest for the nearest cue (blue in Figure 5b, 627 ms) and it increased by 24/30 ms (green/red in Figure 5b) for the more distant cues.
claims.evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claims.claim: In Experiment 2 with scrambled cartoons, the filling-in model made the wrong prediction that RT is shortest near boundaries (r=−0.30).
claims.source: As in experiment 1, the filling-in model made the wrong prediction that RT is shortest near boundaries (r=−0.30).
claims.evidence: This compares model predictions to experimental data.

claims.claim: In Experiment 2 with scrambled cartoons, the Euclidean model showed a weak relationship (r=0.29).
claims.source: The Euclidean model predicts that RT depends on the distance between fixation point and cue (i.e. the eccentricity of the cue) but this relationship was weak in the data (r=0.29).
claims.evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: In Experiment 2 with scrambled cartoons, the predictions of the pixel-by-pixel model were better (r=0.36) than the Euclidean model.
claims.source: The predictions of the pixel-by-pixel model were better (r=0.36) but those of the growth-cone model were best (r=0.76).
claims.evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 5e.

claims.claim: In Experiment 2 with scrambled cartoons, the growth-cone model was best (r=0.76).
claims.source: The predictions of the pixel-by-pixel model were better (r=0.36) but those of the growth-cone model were best (r=0.76).
claims.evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 5f.

claims.claim: In Experiment 2 with scrambled cartoons, the growth-cone model explained 58% of the variance.
claims.source: The growth-cone model explained 58% of the variance, which was significantly better than the other three models (Figure 6a) (bootstrap statistic: all ps<0.01)
claims.evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claims.claim: In Experiment 2 with scrambled cartoons, the growth-cone model was significantly better than the other three models.
claims.source: The growth-cone model explained 58% of the variance, which was significantly better than the other three models (Figure 6a) (bootstrap statistic: all ps<0.01)
claims.evidence: This is supported by bootstrap statistical analysis.

claims.claim: In Experiment 2 with scrambled cartoons, the estimated time per growth cone shift was 24 ms (95% confidence interval; 18–29 ms).
claims.source: the regression yielded an estimated time per growth cone shift of 24 ms (95% confidence interval; 18–29 ms), in accordance with the estimate of Experiment 1.
claims.evidence: This is derived from regression analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: Perceptual grouping of 2D image regions invokes a serial grouping process with a speed that depends on their scale.
claims.source: Thus, perceptual grouping of 2D image regions invokes a serial grouping process with a speed that depends on their scale: wide regions are grouped quickly and narrow regions more slowly.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results of Experiment 2.

claims.claim: In Experiment 2 with cartoon outlines, the growth cone model explained 41% of the variance.
claims.source: We did, however, also test the cartoon images in 22 subjects (Figure 6b). The growth cone model explained 41% of the variance, which is more than any other model (bootstrap: all ps<0.01).
claims.evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 6b.

claims.claim: In Experiment 2 with cartoon outlines, the growth cone model was better than any other model.
claims.source: The growth cone model explained 41% of the variance, which is more than any other model (bootstrap: all ps<0.01).
claims.evidence: This is supported by bootstrap statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The growth cone model was not better than the other models for the detailed cartoons with interior contours and for the color pictures.
claims.source: However, the growth cone model was not better than the other models for the detailed cartoons with interior contours and for the color pictures (Figure 6c,d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figures 6c and 6d.

claims.claim: The interior lines of the detailed cartoons and the colors and textures of the picture stimuli influence grouping speed.
claims.source: These results reveal that the growth-cone model provides an excellent account for the pattern of RTs for scrambled cartoons and cartoon outlines, but that the predictions for the detailed cartoons (with internal contours) and colored pictures are worse. It follows that the interior lines of the detailed cartoons and the colors and textures of the picture stimuli influence grouping speed.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of model fits across different stimulus types.

claims.claim: Grouping depends on the spread of object-based attention across the features that need to be bound in perception.
claims.source: Previous studies suggested that grouping depends on the spread of object-based attention across the features that need to be bound in perception (Rensink, 2000; Roelfsema, 2006; Roelfsema et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Egly et al. (1994) found that if the cue was invalid and the target appeared at the other end of the cued bar, the response was faster than if it appeared at the non-cued bar.
claims.source: Their main finding, however, was that if the cue was invalid and the target appeared at the other end of the cued bar (invalid same-object trials), the response was faster than if it appeared at the non-cued bar (invalid different-object trials), even if the distance between the target and the invalid cue was constant.
claims.evidence: This describes a finding from prior research by Egly et al. (1994).

claims.claim: The reaction-time difference between invalid same- and different object trials is a measure for object-based attention.
claims.source: The reaction-time difference between invalid same- and different object trials is a measure for object-based attention, which is hypothesized to select the entire cued bar (Egly et al., 1994; Xu and Chun, 2007; Lamy and Egeth, 2002; Drummond & Shomstein 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on object-based attention.

claims.claim: In Experiment 3, the average accuracy across participants was 99%.
claims.source: The average accuracy across participants was 99%.
claims.evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claims.claim: In Experiment 3, bar width did not influence RT on validly cued trials.
claims.source: On validly cued trials, bar width did not influence RT (t(10)=−1.450, p>0.1; Figure 7b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7b.

claims.claim: In Experiment 3, RTs were shorter on validly cued than invalidly cued trials.
claims.source: As expected, RTs were shorter on validly cued than invalidly cued trials (t(10)=−3.468, p<0.01).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: In Experiment 3, RTs were shorter with invalid cues on the same object than on a different object.
claims.source: We computed the object-based advantage for the broad and narrow bars and found that RTs were shorter with invalid cues on the same object than on a different object, an object-based advantage that is in accordance with previous studies (Egly et al., 1994; Xu and Chun, 2007; Lamy and Egeth, 2002; Drummond & Shomstein 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and is consistent with prior research.

claims.claim: In Experiment 3, the maximal object-based advantage occurred earlier for the broad bar than for the narrow bar.
claims.source: The maximal object-based advantage occurred earlier for the broad bar than for the narrow bar (Figure 7c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7c.

claims.claim: In Experiment 3, the object-based advantage peaked after 344 ms (95% confidence interval: 311–376 ms) for the broad bar.
claims.source: We fitted a Gaussian function to the object-based benefit and found that it peaked after 344 ms (95% confidence interval: 311–376 ms) for the broad bar
claims.evidence: This is derived from fitting analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: In Experiment 3, the object-based advantage peaked after 463 ms (434–492 ms) for the narrow bar.
claims.source: and after 463 ms (434–492 ms) for the narrow bar (p<0.001; bootstrap analysis).
claims.evidence: This is derived from fitting analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: In Experiment 3, the estimated speed of attention spreading was 31 ms per growth cone.
claims.source: We estimated the speed of attention spreading by dividing the time difference of 119 ms by the difference in the estimated number of growth cones (7.2–3.3=3.9) and obtained a speed of 31 ms per growth cone, compatible with the speed estimates of Experiments 1 and 2.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from experimental data.

claims.claim: The new task revealed that perceptual grouping relies on a serial, incremental process, refuting the uniform connectedness rule proposed by Palmer and Rock, 1994.
claims.source: The new task allowed us to measure the time course of grouping operations in simple 2D line drawings and revealed that perceptual grouping relies on a serial, incremental process, refuting the uniform connectedness rule proposed by Palmer and Rock, 1994.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claims.claim: Some forms of perceptual grouping related to the recognition of objects or image categories is very rapid and pre-attentive.
claims.source: At first sight, such a slow, serial grouping process seems to be at odds with previous findings that some forms of perceptual grouping, related to the recognition of objects or image categories like animals and vehicles, is very rapid and pre-attentive (Thorpe et al., 1996; Kirchner and Thorpe, 2006; Moore and Egeth, 1997; Treisman, 1985).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Pre-attentive formation of perceptual groupings appears to rely on rapid feedforward computations that take place when visual information propagates from early to higher visual areas.
claims.source: The pre-attentive formation of perceptual groupings appears to rely on rapid feedforward computations that take place when visual information propagates from early to higher visual areas (Yamins et al., 2014), a strategy that is also used by state-of-the-art convolutional networks for object recognition (Szegedy et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: The recognition of objects in the scene does not imply that visual segmentation processes have completed.
claims.source: However, the recognition of objects in the scene does not imply that visual segmentation processes have completed (Epshtein et al., 2008; Houtkamp and Roelfsema, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: It is difficult to compute connectedness in a purely feedforward manner.
claims.source: For example, connectedness is one of the cues for perceptual grouping, and it is difficult to compute connectedness in a purely feedforward manner (Minsky and Papert, 1990; Roelfsema et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claims.claim: If a scene contains multiple animals, the recognition of the species does not imply that all parts of every animal have been grouped as coherent percepts.
claims.source: Furthermore, if a scene contains multiple animals, the recognition of the species does not imply that all parts of every animal have been grouped as coherent percepts (Korjoukov et al., 2012) because there are also cases where recognition precedes image parsing (Vecera and Farah, 1997; Peterson et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: The visual system processes simple 2D image regions as miniature mazes.
claims.source: Our results suggest that the visual system processes simple 2D image regions as miniature mazes, and for mazes serial processing is less surprising (Crowe et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results with a citation to related work.

claims.claim: Serial processing has been observed in contour grouping tasks where grouping is associated with the gradual spread of object-based attention over the perceptual group.
claims.source: Serial processing has also been observed previously in contour grouping tasks (Roelfsema, 2006), where grouping is associated with the gradual spread of object-based attention over the perceptual group (Figure 1a,b) (Houtkamp et al., 2003), a process that can only occur for one curve at a time (Houtkamp and Roelfsema, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: In the visual cortex, the spread of attention is associated with the propagation of enhanced neuronal activity over the representation of the relevant curve.
claims.source: In the visual cortex, the spread of attention is associated with the propagation of enhanced neuronal activity over the representation of the relevant curve (Pooresmaeili and Roelfsema, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to neurophysiological research.

claims.claim: Spreading is fast if curves are far apart but it slows down if curves are in each other's vicinity.
claims.source: Spreading is fast if curves are far apart but it slows down if curves are in each other's vicinity.
claims.evidence: This is based on prior research on curve tracing.

claims.claim: The curve-tracing operation has been modeled as a growth-cone process.
claims.source: The curve-tracing operation has also been modeled as a growth-cone process, similar to the one we now used to model grouping of 2D image regions (Pooresmaeili and Roelfsema, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior modeling work.

claims.claim: During object recognition, image parsing may be unnecessary, but during grasping one needs to determine whether surfaces belong to the same object.
claims.source: In daily life, this serial grouping operation may only be necessary for specific tasks. During object recognition, image parsing may be unnecessary, but during grasping one needs to determine whether surfaces belong to the same object to avoid placing fingers on surfaces of different ones.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the functional role of serial grouping.

claims.claim: The variation in the scale of processing could rely on multiple stages of the visual cortical hierarchy where neurons have different RF sizes.
claims.source: The variation in the scale of processing could rely on multiple stages of the visual cortical hierarchy where neurons have different RF sizes (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical proposal illustrated in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Near boundaries and in narrow parts of an object, the perceptual grouping process requires a high spatial resolution, which can be supported by small receptive fields in lower areas.
claims.source: Near boundaries and in narrow parts of an object, the perceptual grouping process requires a high spatial resolution, which can be supported by small receptive fields in lower areas (purple and blue in Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on known properties of visual cortex.

claims.claim: If the homogeneous image regions are larger, the propagation may take place in higher areas with larger RFs so that the grouping speed is higher.
claims.source: If the homogeneous image regions are larger, the propagation may take place in higher areas with larger RFs so that the grouping speed is higher (red in Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on known properties of visual cortex.

claims.claim: The scale dependence of the spread of object-based attention is in accordance with neuroimaging studies revealing the stronger engagement of lower visual areas when the relevant spatial scale is finer.
claims.source: This scale dependence of the spread of object-based attention is in accordance with neuroimaging studies revealing the stronger engagement of lower visual areas when the relevant spatial scale is finer (Rijpkema et al., 2008; Hopf et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to neuroimaging studies.

claims.claim: The growth-cone mechanism does not require the receptive field size to be constant within a visual cortical area.
claims.source: Although the growth-cone model capitalizes on the presence of receptive fields with different sizes at distinct levels of the visual cortical processing hierarchy, it does not require the receptive field size to be constant within a visual cortical area.
claims.evidence: This is a clarification about the model's assumptions.

claims.claim: The size of receptive fields increases with eccentricity.
claims.source: Indeed, it is well known that the size of receptive fields increases with eccentricity.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about visual cortex organization.

claims.claim: The horizontal distance between neurons with abutting, non-overlapping RFs is relatively constant across visual areas.
claims.source: The horizontal distance between neurons with abutting, non-overlapping RFs is relatively constant across visual areas (Harvey and Dumoulin, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: The propagation speed (in °/s or growth-cones/s) should be constant across eccentricities for a bar with a constant width.
claims.source: Thus, if we assume that the propagation of enhanced neuronal activity through horizontal connections is also similar, it follows that the propagation speed (in °/s or growth-cones/s) should also be constant across eccentricities for a bar with a constant width.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of visual cortex.

results.result: Experiment 1 demonstrates that perceptual grouping of wedge-shaped 2D image regions is a serial process where attention spreads fastest in homogeneous areas and slows near edges. The growth-cone model best explains the reaction time patterns (86% variance in Exp 1A, 72% in Exp 1B), significantly outperforming alternative models including uniform connectedness, pixel-by-pixel, filling-in, and Euclidean models. The estimated grouping speed is 22 ms per growth cone.
results.evaluation: The experimental data from Experiment 1 (both 1A and 1B) provide strong, converging evidence for serial perceptual grouping with scale-dependent speed. The statistical analyses (ANOVA, regression, bootstrap tests) are appropriate and show significant effects. The control experiment (C43) rules out masking as an alternative explanation. The growth-cone model's superior fit is demonstrated through rigorous model comparison with multiple baselines.

results.result: Experiment 2 extends the serial grouping findings to more complex stimuli. For scrambled cartoons and cartoon outlines, the growth-cone model explains 58% and 41% of RT variance respectively, significantly outperforming alternative models. The estimated speed (24 ms/growth cone) is consistent with Experiment 1. However, the model performs poorly for detailed cartoons with interior contours and color pictures, indicating that interior features and textures influence grouping speed beyond what the outline-based model captures.
results.evaluation: The results for scrambled cartoons and cartoon outlines strongly support the growth-cone model with appropriate statistical validation (bootstrap tests, p<0.01). The authors appropriately acknowledge the model's limitations for more complex stimuli (C67, C68) and provide a reasonable interpretation. The consistency of speed estimates across experiments strengthens the findings. The limitation is clearly stated rather than hidden, which is scientifically appropriate.

results.result: Experiment 3 directly measures the spread of object-based attention using an Egly cueing paradigm. The object-based advantage (faster RTs for invalid same-object vs. different-object trials) peaks earlier for broad bars (344 ms) than narrow bars (463 ms), with a time difference of 119 ms. This yields an estimated attention spreading speed of 31 ms per growth cone, consistent with Experiments 1 and 2.
results.evaluation: Experiment 3 provides direct evidence linking perceptual grouping to object-based attention spread with appropriate statistical analyses (t-tests, Gaussian fitting, bootstrap confidence intervals). The convergence of speed estimates across all three experiments (22, 24, and 31 ms/growth cone) strengthens the overall conclusion. The experimental design appropriately controls for distance effects by matching cue-target distances across conditions.

results.result: The experimental findings refute the uniform connectedness hypothesis of Palmer and Rock (1994), which predicted instantaneous grouping of uniformly connected regions. Instead, the data demonstrate that perceptual grouping of 2D image regions relies on a serial, incremental process.
results.evaluation: The experimental evidence clearly contradicts the uniform connectedness prediction that RT should be constant across cue locations within a homogeneous region. The systematic RT variations as a function of cue position (C38, C46, C47) and the superior fit of the growth-cone model over constant-RT models provide strong evidence against this prior theory.

results.result: The measured propagation speed of 8-16 cm/s (calculated from 2-4 mm cortical distance per 25 ms) is consistent with neurophysiological measurements of horizontal propagation of neuronal activity in visual cortex.
results.evaluation: The calculation linking behavioral measurements to cortical propagation speed is based on well-established neuroanatomical data (C115, C98) and yields values consistent with prior neurophysiological studies (C116). This provides a plausible neural mechanism for the behavioral findings, though it remains an inference rather than direct neural measurement.

results.result: The authors propose that the visual cortical hierarchy can implement scale-dependent spread of object-based attention by leveraging different receptive field sizes in distinct cortical areas. Near boundaries and in narrow regions, small RFs in lower areas support high-resolution processing; in larger homogeneous regions, larger RFs in higher areas enable faster propagation. This mechanism is compatible with RF size increases with eccentricity and is supported by neuroimaging studies showing stronger engagement of lower visual areas for finer spatial scales.
results.evaluation: This is a theoretical proposal (speculation/inference) rather than a directly tested hypothesis. While it is consistent with known properties of visual cortex organization (C95, C97, C98) and provides a plausible neural implementation, it lacks direct experimental validation in this study. The proposal is reasonable and well-grounded in neuroscience, but would require neurophysiological experiments to confirm. The authors appropriately present this as a discussion point rather than a proven mechanism.

results.result: The authors discuss limitations of the current growth-cone model implementation (based only on outlines) and propose that future models incorporating object recognition through hierarchical convolutional networks and semantic segmentation could better account for grouping with interior features, colors, and textures. They suggest that semantic segmentation networks with horizontal connections could explain serial RT patterns in natural images.
results.evaluation: This is primarily speculative discussion about future model development rather than tested results. While the limitations of the current model are clearly demonstrated (C67, C68, C101), the proposed solutions (C104-C111) are not empirically validated in this study. The discussion appropriately cites relevant computational neuroscience and machine learning work, but these remain proposals for future research rather than supported findings.

results.result: The authors conclude that perceptual grouping of 2D image regions requires tens to hundreds of milliseconds for naturalistic pictures, during which subjects spread object-based attention within image regions. They speculate that the typical fixation duration of 200-300 ms may be optimized to allow time for both object recognition and image parsing.
results.evaluation: The conclusion that grouping takes tens to hundreds of milliseconds (C117) is well-supported by the experimental data across all three experiments. The interpretation that this time is needed for spreading object-based attention (C118) is supported by Experiment 3. However, the speculation about fixation duration optimization (C120) is clearly marked as speculation and is not directly tested, which is appropriate scientific practice.

results.result: The manuscript provides background on visual perception, noting that the visual system creates structured representations by grouping features into objects, but the mechanisms underlying perceptual organization are only partially understood.
results.evaluation: These are accurate statements of established knowledge in visual neuroscience and perception, appropriately setting up the motivation for the study. They represent consensus views in the field rather than novel claims.

results.result: The introduction reviews prior literature on perceptual grouping, distinguishing between rapid, pre-attentive object recognition (which can be fast and feedforward) and slower, serial grouping processes (as in curve tracing). The authors note that curve tracing exhibits size invariance and has been modeled as a growth-cone process, providing precedent for their current work.
results.evaluation: This is an accurate review of prior literature with appropriate citations. The distinction between fast feedforward recognition and slower serial grouping processes is well-established in the field. The discussion of curve tracing and size invariance appropriately contextualizes the current study within existing research.

results.result: The authors describe five computational models for perceptual grouping: uniform connectedness (instantaneous grouping), pixel-by-pixel (constant speed spreading), growth-cone (scale-dependent spreading), filling-in (inward from boundaries), and Euclidean (distance-based). These models make distinct predictions about RT patterns that can be tested experimentally.
results.evaluation: The model descriptions are clear and appropriately grounded in prior literature. The models are well-defined with explicit mathematical formulations provided in the Methods section. The models represent reasonable alternative hypotheses spanning the space of plausible mechanisms, making them appropriate for comparative evaluation.

results.result: The authors review the Egly cueing paradigm and the concept of object-based attention, noting that the RT difference between invalid same-object and different-object trials is an established measure of object-based attention.
results.evaluation: This accurately describes established methodology in the attention literature with appropriate citations. The Egly paradigm is a well-validated approach for measuring object-based attention, making it appropriate for Experiment 3.

results.result: The authors pose the question of whether object recognition affects perceptual grouping by providing larger chunks to be grouped at once, citing prior work suggesting this possibility.
results.evaluation: This is an appropriate research question based on prior literature (C55). While the current study addresses this question partially through Experiment 2 (showing that the model works less well for recognizable objects), it is not fully resolved and is appropriately discussed as requiring future work.

results.result: The authors speculate that serial grouping may only be necessary for specific tasks, such as grasping, where determining whether surfaces belong to the same object is critical, but may be unnecessary for object recognition.
results.evaluation: This is clearly marked as speculation about the functional role of serial grouping in everyday behavior. While plausible, it is not directly tested in the current study and represents a hypothesis for future investigation.
